title: India Just Opened the World's First Nuclear-Powered Hydrogen Plant. No Other Country Has Done This.
excerpt: The Kalpakkam facility uses heat from a fast breeder reactor to split water without burning a single gram of fossil fuel — a technology the rest of the world is still chasing.
body:
At the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research in Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu, something happened last week that no country has managed before: hydrogen was produced using nuclear heat, without any fossil fuels, without any carbon emissions, and without electrolysis.

India's Department of Atomic Energy inaugurated the world's first hydrogen production facility based on the Copper-Chlorine thermochemical cycle — a process that uses heat from a nuclear reactor to drive a chemical reaction that splits water into hydrogen and oxygen. It is, by every measure, a first.

## How It Works

Most of the world's hydrogen today comes from steam methane reforming — essentially, cooking natural gas at high temperatures. It is cheap, proven, and responsible for roughly 830 million tonnes of CO₂ annually. Green hydrogen, produced by splitting water using renewable electricity, is cleaner but expensive and energy-intensive.

The Kalpakkam facility takes a third path. The Copper-Chlorine (Cu-Cl) thermochemical cycle uses process heat — not electricity — from the Fast Breeder Test Reactor (FBTR) to drive a series of chemical reactions at relatively low temperatures (around 530°C). The result is hydrogen production that requires no fossil fuels and no electrolysis, making it potentially more efficient than both grey and green hydrogen at scale.

"The successful integration of nuclear process heat with hydrogen generation marks a pioneering technological breakthrough," the DAE said in its official statement, calling it a "promising pathway for large-scale, carbon-free hydrogen production using advanced nuclear reactors."



> **"India's DAE has signalled that the Kalpakkam facility is a "technology demonstrator," with commercial-scale production as the next step."**


The facility was inaugurated by Ajit Kumar Mohanty, Secretary of the DAE and Chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission, alongside Sreekumar G. Pillai, Director of IGCAR.

## Why It Matters


![Tamil Nadu — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f2/Mamallapuram_view.jpg)


Hydrogen is widely considered the missing piece in the clean energy puzzle. It can power steel plants, fertiliser factories, heavy trucks, and shipping — sectors where batteries alone cannot do the job. India's National Green Hydrogen Mission, launched in 2023 with a ₹19,744 crore outlay, aims to make the country a global hub for green hydrogen production and export.

But production costs remain the central challenge. Green hydrogen currently costs between $4 and $6 per kilogram in India, well above the $1-$2 range needed to compete with fossil-fuel-derived hydrogen. Nuclear thermochemical production could dramatically lower that floor because fast reactors generate heat continuously, independent of weather or time of day, and the Cu-Cl cycle operates at significantly lower temperatures than competing thermochemical processes.

The technology was developed indigenously by the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) in Mumbai. IGCAR and BARC collaborated on the research, process development, engineering design, and commissioning — a multi-year effort that culminated in the facility's inauguration on June 26.

## India's Nuclear Edge

India is one of the few countries with an operational fast breeder reactor programme. The FBTR at Kalpakkam has been running since 1985, and the larger 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) is expected to reach criticality soon. Fast reactors are uniquely suited for thermochemical hydrogen production because they operate at higher temperatures than conventional pressurised water reactors, providing the process heat that drives the Cu-Cl cycle.

Countries including the US, Canada, South Korea, and Japan have been researching the Cu-Cl cycle for years, but none have achieved the integration of nuclear process heat with a working hydrogen production facility. India's demonstration puts it at the front of the global queue.

## The Diaspora Connection

For NRIs working in clean energy, nuclear engineering, and hydrogen infrastructure — a rapidly growing cohort across North America and Europe — this is more than a technical milestone. It signals that India is building the foundational technology for a hydrogen economy, creating potential corridors for technology transfer, joint ventures, and talent circulation between the diaspora and India's research establishment.

India's DAE has signalled that the Kalpakkam facility is a "technology demonstrator," with commercial-scale production as the next step. If the economics hold, nuclear hydrogen could become India's answer to the clean energy transition — and a technology it exports rather than imports.

*Sources: Department of Atomic Energy (India), ANI, IANS, Energetica India, TBS News*
